entities.summary:
Flavius Bauto, a Romanised Frankish general, emerged as a dominant military and political force in the Western Roman Empire during the late 4th century CE, specifically from approximately 383 to his death in 388 CE. Serving as *magister militum praesentalis*, Bauto was instrumental in stabilizing the court of the young emperor Valentinian II, effectively acting as a regent and a bulwark against internal and external threats. His career exemplifies the increasing prominence of Germanic commanders within the Roman military hierarchy, a trend that profoundly reshaped imperial power dynamics and contributed to the eventual fragmentation of the Western Empire.

Bauto's most significant actions centered on defending the legitimacy of Valentinian II against the usurper Magnus Maximus. After the assassination of Emperor Gratian in 383 CE, Bauto, alongside other loyalists, secured Valentinian's position in Milan and later orchestrated a critical alliance with Emperor Theodosius I of the East. This alliance culminated in Theodosius's decisive campaign against Maximus in 388 CE, which restored Valentinian II to full authority in the West. Bauto's military prowess was also evident in his campaigns against the Alamanni, demonstrating his commitment to Roman territorial integrity despite his Germanic origins. He strategically positioned his protégé, Arbogast, for future power, ensuring a continuity of influence for Frankish generals.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Flavius Bauto's actions were critical in preserving the Western Roman throne for Valentinian II during a period of intense crisis, directly influencing the political landscape of the late 4th century. His career exemplifies the growing power of Germanic generals that profoundly shaped the ultimate decline of the Western Roman Empire.
